messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: user-supplied scales
parts:
This comes up a lot. I have a parameter that I know is not anywhere near unit scale, for example I think it's around 100 or 200. So, sure, I can do something like this:
parameters {
real a_adj;
}
transformed parameters {
real a;
a <- 150 + 50*a_adj;
}
and then I'll be ok. But this is awkward as I have to define a new parameter, come up with a new name, etc. What I'd really like is for Stan to do this. I think this should be possible. For now let's just talk about unbounded parameters. Currently the default in Stan is to scale all parameters using center 0 and scale 1; that is, to take the parameter on origional scale, subtract 0, and divide by 1. But why not have the option to subtract M and divide by S?

For example,
parameters {
real<center=150, scale=50> a;
}

As I said, this comes up with a lot of models and it's awkward to be hacking this by doing linear transformations in R or Stan.

A


P.S. I used to put these sorts of things on dev list but now dev is on this horrible "discourse" server where I can't follow the threads, so I'm using stan-users so I can read the replies that people send me. Also, I think users might be interested in this.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] user-supplied scales
parts:
I get what you're trying to do, but I can't tell what you intend
the value of a to be. That is, are you going to want to write

a ~ normal(0, 1);

or is it

a ~ normal(150, 50);

If it's not the latter, then it's going to be very confusing. If
it is the latter, then this works a lot like our other transforms,
but it's simpler in that it has a constant log Jacobian.

For now, you could define a function that combines the unit normal
and rescaling and translating:

real scaled_std_normal_lp(real a_std, real c, real s) {
a_std ~ normal(0, 1);
return c + s * a_std;
}

Then usage would be:

parameters {
real a_std;
...
model {
real a = scaled_std_normal_lp(a_std, 150, 50);
...

That way, it's clear that a_std is the one on the standard scale and
the function name provides a hint that you're using a standard normal
distribution on a_std and rescaling it to produce a.

It seems more natural to define a in the transformed parameters block,
but we can't get the unit normal in there because we can't access the
target.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] user-supplied scales
parts:
Hi, yes, in that example I wanted to give the prior a ~ normal(150,50); but then this parameter is not on unit scale. Maybe not such a huge problem with normal(150,50) but could create real problems if it was normal(150,2) or, for that matter, normal(0.0002, 0.0001). What I'd really like is to for the linear transformation to be part of the declaration of "a", because then as a user I would not need to define a_std etc. Also it's actually not so important to me that the prior be in there; to me, the big deal is that I'd like the scaling to be right in the transformation directly.
In some sense this relates to a larger question of how to think about scaling and express it in the language.
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] user-supplied scales
parts:
OK, then a few more questions and comments.

1. Do you want just a center and just a scale as options, or
if they show up, would both be required?

2. Can they occur with lower and upper bounds? If so, the center
and scale seem to make most sense on the unconstrained scale. Right
now, we have sigma_unc in (-inf, inf), and it transforms for <lower=0>
to

sigma = exp(sigma_conc)

So that if we have

real<lower=0, center=20, scale=5> sigma;

it would produce the transformed type:

sigma = exp(5 * sigma_unc + 20)

3. We would probably want to allow parameters as values of
center and scale. Then we start getting Jacobians we need
to worry about because they may be constant in the transformed
parameter, but not in other parameters used to define bounds.

4. What types other than real should these work for? I'm thinking
the ones that are unbounded make most sense: ordered, pos_ordered, cov_matrix
(and of course, vector, row_vector, and matrix).

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] user-supplied scales
parts:
3.  We would probably want to allow parameters as values of
center and scale.  Then we start getting Jacobians we need
to worry about because they may be constant in the transformed
parameter, but not in other parameters used to define bounds.

Do we though?  If we’re thinking about this purely as a means
of standardizing parameters then why not limit the locations and
scales to data?

4.  What types other than real should these work for?  I'm thinking
the ones that are unbounded make most sense: ordered, pos_ordered, cov_matrix
(and of course, vector, row_vector, and matrix).

We can avoid the potential confusion between constrained and
unconstrained scales entirely by limiting <center=, scale=> to 
unconstrained scalar parameters.

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] user-supplied scales
parts: On Feb 26, 2017, at 6:36 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

3.  We would probably want to allow parameters as values of
center and scale.  Then we start getting Jacobians we need
to worry about because they may be constant in the transformed
parameter, but not in other parameters used to define bounds.

Do we though?  If we’re thinking about this purely as a means
of standardizing parameters then why not limit the locations and
scales to data?

I was thinking of only allowing these locations and scales to be data.  Allowing them to be parameters is interesting but it's an idea I haven't fully thought through.  Only allowing as data would solve most of our use cases, I think.

4.  What types other than real should these work for?  I'm thinking
the ones that are unbounded make most sense: ordered, pos_ordered, cov_matrix
(and of course, vector, row_vector, and matrix).

We can avoid the potential confusion between constrained and
unconstrained scales entirely by limiting <center=, scale=> to 
unconstrained scalar parameters.

It would be fine with me to just allow it for unconstrained parameters.  We could also have log_center and log_scale for parameters constrained to be positive.  But in such settings it wouldn't kill the user to just define the parameter on the log scale.

I would, however, like to allow scales on vectors and matrices of unscaled parameters.  That could make sense.  Just for a simple example, imagine a model in which there are latent continuous test scores for each student.  We might want all these to be scaled with center=50 and scale=25, say.
